claims.text: The onset of premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by the degree of surface segregation of low-melting-point elements.
Surface segregation of low-melting-point elements forms a disordered, liquid-like surface layer.
The disordered, liquid-like surface layer destabilizes the nanoparticle's crystalline structure.
Increasing the concentration of a low-melting-point element promotes its surface segregation.
Higher surface concentrations of low-melting-point species destabilize surface crystalline order.
Destabilization of surface crystalline order lowers the local melting point.
A low-melting-point-element-enriched surface initiates a liquid-like phase that propagates into full melting as temperature increases.
Higher low-melting-point-element content and smaller particle size produce enhanced surface segregation.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will have a statistically significant reduction in premelting-onset temperature relative to more homogeneous, larger nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will have a statistically significant reduction in complete-melting temperature relative to more homogeneous, larger nanoparticles.
In larger nanoparticles with even elemental distributions, surface contributions are minimized and melting is dominated by bulk properties.
The proposed mechanism should apply when nanoparticles are sufficiently small and their compositions foster moderate-to-high surface segregation.
Bulk melting behavior may dominate in larger nanoparticles or nanoparticles with extremely homogeneous compositions.
The quantitative relationship among low-melting-point-element concentration, surface segregation, and melting-temperature reduction is not yet determined.
